answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Green Strategies welcomes the Protocol’s efforts to develop consequential accounting, and Green Strategies has advocated for consequential accounting to become a key component of updating and modernizing Scope 2 reporting[1][2]. Consequential accounting enables reporting companies to distinguish transactions that have higher GHG reduction impact from those with lesser impact and to target transactions and investments at locations and times that are most GHG-intensive. Consequential accounting can complement the preparation of location-based and market-based inventories. Actions that may lower a Scope 2 market-based inventory, such as matching a zero-emission EAC to a megawatt-hour of consumption, may have varying real-world impact depending the time and location of the EAC’s underlying generation. Consequential accounting considers how and the extent to which a clean energy project achieves incremental reduction in fossil generation and takes into account project characteristics (e.g. new build) and the timing and location of the project’s generation.

In 2025, Green Strategies surveyed a group of leading corporate clean energy buyers to understand their perspective and interest in consequential accounting [3]. The survey asked respondents to consider a scenario where a GHG accounting system allows buyers the flexibility to procure outside of their current market boundaries and recognizes avoided emissions impact (the scenario specified that avoided emissions would be reported next to, but separate from, Scope 2 inventories). The survey found that approximately 60% of respondents would procure outside of their existing market boundaries. Respondents stated interest in procurement opportunities that would displace more GHG emissions (e.g. they operate in relatively clean grids already) and pointed to procurement challenges within their current market boundaries, such as restrictions on customer access to clean electricity.

In providing guidance for consequential accounting, there are important considerations for standardizing calculations, data, and disclosure. The Protocol should continue to work with stakeholders to refine methodologies and formats for consequential impact reporting. We believe the consequential accounting subgroup of the Scope 2 Technical Working Group (TWG) was on the right track in developing a transparent and credible approach to consequential accounting[4].

[1] Modernizing How Electricity Buyers Account and are Recognized for Decarbonization Impact and Climate Leadership. 2022.
https://cdn.catf.us/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/16103856/corporate-electricity-procurement-report.pdf

[2] Modernizing GHG Accounting Rules and Climate Leadership Programs. How Attributional and Consequential Accounting Differ and Why Both are Essential to Measure and Incentivize Progress Towards GHG Reduction Goals.
https://tinyurl.com/35f8cv29

[3] How Scope 2 Revisions May Change Clean Electricity Procurement Strategies.
https://www.greenstrategies.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Practitioner-Insights-Scope-2-Clean-Electricity-Revisions.pdf

[4] Public Statement from Members of the GHG Protocol Scope 2 TWG Consequential Subgroup. https://marginalimpactmethod.org/

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The proposed formula is helpful in establishing how consequential impact from clean electricity projects would begin to quantify impact, but it is also incomplete. The formula does not incorporate the calculation of a company’s induced emissions from consumption nor the netting of avoided emissions from procurement and induced emissions. These components are necessary so that a company and external users of consequential disclosures can understand the baseline from which a company is operating and the relative ambition of a company’s procurement versus its consumption. Green Strategies in partnership with the Clean Air Task Force and the NorthBridge Group[1] is one of several entities who have outlined such an approach [2][3][4].

[1] Modernizing How Electricity Buyers Account and are Recognized for Decarbonization Impact and Climate Leadership
https://cdn.catf.us/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/16103856/corporate-electricity-procurement-report.pdf

[2] WattTime: Accounting for Impact, https://watttime.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/WattTimeAccountingForImpact-202209-vFinal2.pdf

[3] RE-Source: Carbon Matching https://www.emissionsfirst.com/_files/ugd/820a9e_23bdd35c3c65419a9501ceaf32cc1d40.pdf

[4] Public Statement from Members of the GHG Protocol Scope 2 TWG Consequential Subgroup, November 2025, https://marginalimpactmethod.org/

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: The formula should focus on primary effects only.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Calculating and reporting avoided emissions impact each year of a project would be helpful since it would allow for a project to identify and indicate any change in the displaced marginal resource that occurs during the project’s lifetime.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
We encourage the Protocol to establish multiple options for demonstrating additionality and for such options to be transparent and clear. The Consequential Accounting subgroup of the Scope 2 TWG recommended establishing additionality through a Regulatory Test, a Timing Test, and either a Positive List OR a Financial Test [1].

[1] Appendix to Public Statement from Members of the GHG Protocol Scope 2 TWG Consequential Subgroup, November 2025, https://marginalimpactmethod.org/Appendix_Table.pdf

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
There is emerging expert consensus that there should be a preference for observable data in consequential analysis, and the methods selected above incorporate such data. We point to the discussion of the ZEROgrid Initiative’s Impact Advisory Initiative: “A Standardized Approach using Observable Data Would Limit the Opportunity for Confusion and Manipulation: The calculation methodology would ideally be standardized and unambiguous so as to mitigate potential confusion, enable replicability, and avoid the potential for individual actors to modify how they implement the metric to improperly inflate the estimated impact of their actions.”[1]

[1] https://zerogrid.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2025/05/iai-performance-metric-principles.pdf

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
We highlight the ZEROgrid Impact Advisory Initiative’s discussion: “Consequential assessment can be conducted using a variety of approaches, including capacity expansion models, yet these approaches are often complex, time-intensive, and subject to producing variable results based upon key inputs and assumptions.”[1]

[1] ZEROgrid’s Impact Advisory Initiative’s Performance Metric Principles, https://zerogrid.org/wpcontent/uploads/dlm_uploads/2025/05/iai-performance-metric-principles.pdf

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text:
There is emerging expert consensus that nodal granularity is appropriate and feasible in estimating emissions impact. See:

- Quantifying the impact of energy system model resolution on siting, cost, reliability, and emissions for electricity generation - https://www.researchgate.net/publication/383010871_Quantifying_the_impact_of_energy_system_model_resolution_on_siting_cost_reliability_and_emissions_for_electricity_generation
- ZeroGrid Expert Consensus Support for a Rigorous Definition of “Deliverability” in Scope 2 GHG Accounting, https://zerogrid.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/2025/05/iai-deliverability-memo.pdf
- Sofia, Sarah, and Yury Dvorkin. "Carbon Impact of Intra-Regional Transmission Congestion." Cell Reports Sustainability. Accepted.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: There is emerging expert consensus that hourly provides the most accurate and temporal granularity in estimating marginal emissions.

answers.label: Appropriate margin weighting approaches
selections: Default 0.50 build margin weight for all projects
GHG Protocol Guidelines for Quantifying GHG Reductions from Grid-connected Electricity Projects

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text:
We point to the recommendations of WattTime[1] and the consequential accounting subgroup of the Scope 2 TWG[2] which suggest a 50/50 weighting as a defensible split. The subgroup proposed “an initial default weight of 0.5 proposed to avoid cherry picking or gaming” and recommended further research to assess whether adjustments or differentiations in weighting would be appropriate in the future.


[1] https://watttime.org/news-and-insights/how-to-use-the-ghg-protocols-optional-consequential-electricity-emissions-reporting-option/

[2] https://marginalimpactmethod.org/Appendix_Table.pdf
